title: Classical pro-etale stalks: strict localization and exactness
statement:
Let $T$ be a scheme, let $\bar t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ be a geometric point [def-weil-geometric-point], and let $T_{(\bar t)}=\operatorname{Spec}A^{\mathrm{sh}}_{T,\bar t}$ be the strict localization constructed as the limit of affine pointed etale neighbourhoods in [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. Work in the small skeleton and universes of $T_{\mathrm{proet}}$ [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site]. The canonical map $T_{(\bar t)}\to T$ is an object of this site. For every sheaf $\mathcal H$ of sets or abelian groups on $T_{\mathrm{proet}}$, evaluation gives an isomorphism
$$\mathcal H(T_{(\bar t)})\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal H_{\bar t},$$
natural in $\mathcal H$, where the stalk is the colimit over all pointed weakly etale neighbourhoods [def-weil-proetale-geometric-stalk]. The functor $\mathcal H\mapsto\mathcal H_{\bar t}$ on abelian sheaves is exact: it preserves finite limits and finite colimits.

source.place: Tag 0993, lemma-classical-point; Tag 0991, section-points, paragraph defining geometric stalks before lemma-classical-point

proof.text: Put $A=A^{\mathrm{sh}}_{T,\bar t}$, $L=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and let $j:L\to T$ be the structural map. Clause (1) of the strict-henselization functoriality theorem supplies the strictly henselian local structure on $A$ and the geometric lift $\lambda:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to L$ at its closed point, with $j\lambda=\bar t$. Choose an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}R\to T$ through $t$. Its pointed lift is one of the affine neighbourhoods in the limit construction, so its limit projection factors $j$ through this open. The affine-chart ind-etale theorem makes its ring map $R\to A$ ind-etale, hence weakly etale by ind-etale stability. The explicit ring/scheme equivalence in the ind-etale-algebra definition makes $L\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ weakly etale. An open immersion is etale by the open-immersion theorem. The comparison-morphism node explicitly states that the inclusion sends every etale $T$-scheme to a weakly etale $T$-scheme, so the affine-open inclusion into $T$ is weakly etale. Composition is weakly etale. Thus $j$ is weakly etale and gives an object of the chosen pro-etale site, transported to its skeleton if necessary. Its size is the size of the small ring colimit in the strict-localization construction.

source.place: Tag 0993, lemma-classical-point, proof; Tag 0991, section-points, geometric-stalk paragraph

proof.text: Let $(U,\bar u)$ be a pointed weakly etale neighbourhood of $\bar t$. Pull it back to $L$: $P=U\times_TL\to L$ is weakly etale by base change, and $(\bar u,\lambda)$ is its marked $\Omega$-point. Choose an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B\subset P$ containing its image $q$. Source-open locality makes $\operatorname{Spec}B\to L$ weakly etale, hence $a:A\to B$ is weakly etale by the explicit ring/scheme equivalence in the ind-etale-algebra definition. The map $A\to B_q$ is weakly etale by weakly etale localization and composition. It is a local map because $q$ lies over the maximal ideal of $A$. Olivier therefore says that $e:A\to B_q$ is an isomorphism. The map $B\to B_q\xrightarrow{e^{-1}}A$ defines a section $L\to P$, and projection gives a $T$-map $\alpha_U:L\to U$. This preserves the geometric point as a morphism, not just its image: writing $\chi:B\to\Omega$ for the marked point and $\theta:A\to\Omega$ for $\lambda$, one has $\chi a=\theta$ and $\ker\chi=q$. Thus $\chi$ extends uniquely to $\chi_q:B_q\to\Omega$; since $\chi_qe=\theta$, we have $\theta e^{-1}(B\to B_q)=\chi$, as required.

source.place: Tag 0993, lemma-classical-point, proof; Tag 0991, section-points, geometric-stalk paragraph

proof.text: The pointed map $\alpha_U$ is unique. Indeed a second such map gives a second section of $P\to L$ through the same marked point $q$. Both sections factor through the affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B$ chosen in step 2: the inverse image of that open contains the closed point of $L$, and an open of a local spectrum containing the closed point is the entire spectrum (if a basic open $D(a)$ contains the maximal ideal, $a$ is a unit). Their ring maps $r:B\to A$ have $r^{-1}(\mathfrak m_A)=q$, hence extend to $r_q:B_q\to A$. Since they are sections, $r_qe=\mathrm{id}_A$; the isomorphism $e$ forces $r_q=e^{-1}$ for both. Consequently the sections and their projections to $U$ agree. In particular the only pointed endomorphism of $(L,\lambda)$ is the identity. For every pointed arrow $v:U\to V$, uniqueness gives $v\alpha_U=\alpha_V$. Thus $(L,\lambda)$ is initial in the category of all pointed weakly etale neighbourhoods.

source.place: Tag 0993, lemma-classical-point, proof; Tag 0991, section-points, geometric-stalk paragraph

proof.text: Apply the definition of the stalk to the opposite neighbourhood category. Its object $(L,\lambda)$ is terminal by step 3. The restriction maps $\mathcal H(U)\xrightarrow{\mathcal H(\alpha_U)}\mathcal H(L)$ form a cocone by $v\alpha_U=\alpha_V$. For any cocone with vertex $M$, its leg at $L$ is the unique map $\mathcal H(L)\to M$ factoring all other legs, because the cocone equation for $\alpha_U$ is precisely this factorization. Hence $\mathcal H(L)$ is the colimit, in sets or abelian groups. The canonical coprojection $\mathcal H(L)\to\mathcal H_{\bar t}$ is the asserted isomorphism. For a sheaf morphism $\eta:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$, naturality of restrictions gives $\eta_L\mathcal H(\alpha_U)=\mathcal K(\alpha_U)\eta_U$; the colimit universal property gives naturality of the isomorphism. No cofinality of etale neighbourhoods inside pro-etale neighbourhoods is used.

source.place: Tag 0993, lemma-classical-point, proof; Tag 0991, section-points, geometric-stalk paragraph

proof.text: Every pro-etale covering $\{W_i\to L\}$ has a section in some member. The covering condition supplies a point $w\in W_i$ over the closed point of $L$. Choose an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}B\subset W_i$ through $w$, with prime $q$. Each covering arrow is weakly etale by the site definition. Source-open locality and the affine ring criterion make $A\to B$ weakly etale, and localization and composition make the local map $A\to B_q$ weakly etale. Olivier applies because $A$ is strictly henselian and $q$ contracts to its maximal ideal, so this local ring map is an isomorphism (no choice of a geometric lift of $w$ is needed). Writing $e:A\to B_q$ for this isomorphism, the ring map $B\to B_q\xrightarrow{e^{-1}}A$ defines $L\to\operatorname{Spec}B\subset W_i$; its composite to $L$ is the identity because $e^{-1}e=\mathrm{id}_A$. This is the required section $\sigma:L\to W_i$. Now let $\varphi:\mathcal G\to\mathcal H$ be an epimorphism of abelian sheaves and $h\in\mathcal H(L)$. The general-site local-surjectivity lemma supplies a covering and lifts $g_i\in\mathcal G(W_i)$ of $h|_{W_i}$. For the split member, $\mathcal G(\sigma)(g_i)$ maps to $h$, by naturality and $\mathcal H(\sigma)\mathcal H(W_i\to L)=\mathrm{id}$. Thus evaluation at $L$ preserves epimorphisms. The sheafification-exactness theorem, clause (1), says that kernels and all limits of abelian sheaves are computed sectionwise, so evaluation preserves finite limits as well.

source.place: Tag 0993, lemma-classical-point, proof; Tag 0991, section-points, geometric-stalk paragraph

proof.text: Evaluation is additive, since addition of sheaf morphisms is sectionwise. It preserves finite biproducts and kernels, and step 5 shows it preserves epimorphisms. For an arbitrary $f:F\to G$, factor it in the abelian sheaf category as $F\twoheadrightarrow I\hookrightarrow G$, and put $Q=\operatorname{coker}f$. The exact sequence $0\to I\to G\to Q\to0$ stays exact: left exactness gives its kernel, and preservation of epimorphisms makes the last map surjective; likewise $F(L)\to I(L)$ is surjective. Therefore $Q(L)=G(L)/f_L(F(L))$, which proves preservation of cokernels. A finite colimit in an additive category is the cokernel of the difference of the two maps between the finite sums of diagram objects and arrow-source objects; these sums and cokernels are preserved. Thus evaluation preserves finite colimits. The natural isomorphism in step 4 transfers finite-limit and finite-colimit preservation to the geometric stalk functor, proving exactness.
